Macramé: Knotted Décor That Sells

Macramé turns ordinary cord into wall art, plant hangers and table pieces using a small set of knots. In this module you will choose the right cord, master six working knots, calculate how much cord a project needs, and finish pieces neatly enough to sell.

Macramé is a way of making textiles by **knotting** cords instead of weaving or sewing them. Every macramé piece, from a small key holder to a two-metre wall hanging, is built from a handful of knots repeated in patterns. If you can tie six knots evenly, you can make almost everything in this module.

Cord thickness is given in millimetres. **3 mm** cord is good for small pieces such as coasters and keyrings. **4 to 5 mm** is the most common size for wall hangings and plant hangers. **6 mm and above** gives a bold, chunky look but uses cord quickly. Buy from craft suppliers or check the rope sellers in your local market, and always feel the cord first: cotton is soft and takes dye; nylon and polypropylene are shiny, slippery and harder to knot evenly.
The six working knots

**Lark's head knot**: fold a cord in half, place the loop over the dowel or ring, bring it behind, then pull both ends through the loop. This mounts cords and gives you two working strands from each cord.

**Square knot**: work with four strands. The middle two are filler cords that stay still. Cross the left cord over the fillers and under the right cord; take the right cord under the fillers and up through the left loop; pull. Repeat in mirror image (start from the right). The finished knot lies flat.
**Half square knot**: tie only the first half of the square knot again and again. The knots twist naturally into a spiral.
**Double half hitch**: hold one cord tight across the others as a guide. Wrap each working cord around the guide twice. A row of these makes a raised line, straight or diagonal.
**Overhand knot**: a simple loop pulled tight, used to stop fringe ends or to make decorative bumps.

**Gathering (wrap) knot**: binds a bundle of cords together, used at the top and bottom of plant hangers. Wrap a separate cord tightly around the bundle, tuck the end through a loop, and pull the loop up under the wraps.

How much cord to cut

Running out of cord in the middle of a piece is the most common beginner frustration, because joining new cord in the middle rarely looks neat. A widely used starting rule is to allow **about 4 times the finished length for each working strand**. Because a lark's head folds each cord in half, you cut each cord about **8 times** the finished length. Dense knotting such as many square knots in a row uses more cord, so add extra; open, airy designs use less. Keep notes of what you actually used, so your own rule improves with every piece.

A wall hanging is the best-known macramé product and the one buyers most often ask for to decorate living rooms, bedrooms, short-let apartments and event backdrops. A good hanging has a **clear shape**, a **focal section** where the eye rests, and **clean finishing** at the dowel and fringe. In this lesson you plan and make a medium hanging from start to finish.

Plan before you knot

Draw the hanging on paper at a small scale, for example 1 cm on paper to 5 cm in real life. Mark three zones: the **header** (top 10 to 15 cm, usually a row of hitches or square knots that holds the cords in order), the **body** (the main pattern), and the **fringe** (loose ends, often cut into a V, a curve or a straight line). Write the knot used in each zone. A clear sketch saves cord, because you can count knots and estimate length before cutting.

Alternating square knots

The **alternating square knot** pattern is the backbone of many hangings. In row 1 you tie square knots across using strands 1 to 4, 5 to 8, and so on. In row 2 you leave out the first two strands and tie with strands 3 to 6, 7 to 10, and so on, so each new knot sits between two knots above it. Row 3 goes back to the row 1 pattern. The result is a net that can be tight (knots close together) or open (leave a gap of 1 to 2 cm between rows). To form a downward V, drop two strands from each side on every new row.
Diagonal hitch lines

Double half hitches tied over a diagonal guide cord make crisp lines that frame the body. Hold the outermost strand at an angle across the others as the guide. Tie each strand onto it with two wraps. Keep the guide cord pulled tight at the same angle for the whole row, or the line will curve. Two hitch lines meeting in the middle form a diamond, which is a strong focal point.

Below the diamond: a 10 cm spiral of half square knots in the centre four strands as the focal detail.

Professional finishing
**Dowel**: sand rough ends; you can stain, paint or wrap the dowel in cord. Upcycled options include a straight, dry tree branch, an old broom handle cut to length or a curtain rod off-cut.
**Hanging cord**: tie a separate cord to both ends of the dowel with a few wraps, so the piece hangs level.
**Fringe**: unravel 3-ply cord with your fingers, brush it with a comb, then cut with very sharp scissors. Wet the fringe slightly and let it dry hanging, to straighten it.
**Stiffening**: for a crisp fringe shape, mist it lightly with a mix of water and a little PVA glue or fabric stiffener, then let it dry before final trimming.
Check every row before moving on

A missed knot or a strand used twice becomes obvious once the piece hangs, and is hard to undo many rows later. After each row, count the knots against your sketch and look at the piece from two metres away.

Plant hangers are practical, quick to make and easy to sell, especially to people in flats with small balconies. Table pieces such as runners and coasters use the same knots on a flat surface. This lesson teaches both, with attention to the one thing a wall hanging never has to do: **carry weight safely**.
A green plant in a pot
A hanger is a product that carries weight, so strength matters as much as looks.
Anatomy of a four-arm plant hanger
Pass 8 cords through a metal or wooden ring and fold them so the ring sits at the middle: you now have 16 strands.
Tie a gathering knot just below the ring to bind all 16 strands together.
Divide the strands into 4 groups of 4. Each group becomes one arm.
In each arm, tie a section of square knots or half square knot spirals, for example 15 to 25 cm.
Below the arms, form the basket: take 2 strands from one arm and 2 from the next arm and tie a square knot joining them, about 8 to 10 cm below the arm knots. Go all the way round.
Make a second row of joining knots 6 to 8 cm lower, then gather all strands with a second gathering knot and trim the tail.

Sizing the basket to the pot

Measure around the widest part of the pot (its circumference). The joined cords must wrap around the pot without slipping. A simple check: the distance between joining knots around the basket, added together, should be close to the circumference. If the gaps are too large, the pot falls through; too small, and the pot sits on top and tips. Always make the hanger with the pot in hand and test the fit before the bottom gathering knot is tightened.

Weight and hooks

A wet pot of soil is much heavier than it looks. Use braided or 4 to 5 mm cotton cord, a solid metal or hardwood ring, and tell buyers to hang it from a ceiling hook fixed into a joist, a solid beam or a wall bracket rated for the load, never from a curtain rod or a plastic hook. Do not hang plants over beds, baby cots or walkways where someone could be hurt if it falls.
Flat pieces: runners and coasters

A **table runner** is a long panel of alternating square knots, worked flat. Instead of a dowel, mount the cords on a temporary stick and remove it at the end, finishing both ends with an overhand-knot fringe. A runner 30 cm wide and 150 cm long on a dining table is a common size, but measure the table: a runner is often about one third of the table's width and hangs over each end by 15 to 30 cm. **Coasters** are small circles or squares, about 10 to 12 cm, made from 3 mm cord. Coil spirals or square-knot squares both work.

Choosing and thinning your paper
**Printed paper napkins**: very thin, so edges vanish. Peel away the plain white back layers and keep only the printed top layer.
**Rice or tissue paper**: strong but thin; good for large areas.
**Magazine pages and old book pages**: thicker; make them thinner by sealing the front with one coat of sealer, then soaking and gently rubbing paper off the back.
**Printed photocopies**: use laser or photocopy prints; many inkjet prints smear when wet, so seal them first and test.
**Fabric such as ankara**: cut with sharp scissors; stiffen first with diluted PVA so it does not fray.
The application method
Tear or cut your design. Torn edges blend into the background better than straight cut edges.
Brush a thin coat of decoupage medium (or PVA glue diluted about 3 parts glue to 1 part water) onto the surface, not the paper.
Lay the paper on, then smooth it from the centre outwards with a soft brush, or press through a sheet of cling film with your fingers to push out air.
Let it dry fully, usually 20 to 30 minutes in Nigerian heat; longer in the rainy season.
Apply a thin top coat of medium over the whole area. Let it dry, then add more coats, each brushed in a different direction.

Burying the edge

After about four coats, sand lightly with fine wet-and-dry paper (for example 400 grit), dipped in water, using very gentle pressure. You are only flattening ridges, not reaching the paper. Wipe clean, let dry, then coat again. Experienced decoupage makers often build up eight to ten coats or more on trays for a glass-smooth feel. If you sand through to the paper, stop, let it dry and add more coats over that area.

Not for food contact or soaking

PVA glue, decoupage medium and most varnishes are not tested as safe for direct contact with food, and decoupage softens if soaked. Do not sell decoupage plates, bowls or cups for eating. Decorate the back of clear glass plates or the outside of jars only, and label items 'wipe clean, do not soak, decorative use'.
Choosing a sealer

For indoor décor, water-based acrylic varnish or polyurethane is easy to use and has low smell. Some clear sealers turn slightly yellow over time, especially oil-based ones, which shows on white backgrounds; test on a sample board and leave it in a sunny window for a few weeks. For outdoor items, choose a sealer labelled for exterior use and expect to reseal. Always read the tin: dry time, recoat time and ventilation instructions differ by brand.
Work in a dust-free corner. A single fly or speck of dust in wet varnish ruins the smooth finish. Cover drying pieces loosely with an upturned clean box, raised on blocks so air can move.

Water-based paints dry quickly, smell less and are easier for a home workspace. Oil-based paints are tougher but need ventilation and solvent clean-up. Never mix water-based and oil-based paint in the same tin.
Five finishes to master

**Dry brushing**: dip only the tips of a dry brush in paint, wipe most of it off on paper, then sweep lightly across the surface. Paint catches only on raised parts, highlighting carvings and texture.
**Colour wash**: thin paint with water (for example 1 part paint to 3 or 4 parts water), brush on and wipe with a cloth. Wood grain shows through softly.
**Sponging**: dab a natural or kitchen sponge in a second colour, blot it, then press onto a dry base coat. Rotate the sponge to avoid a repeating mark. Good for a stone look.
**Distressing**: paint a dark base, then a light top coat. When dry, sand edges and corners where natural wear would happen, so the dark colour shows.

**Crackle**: paint a base colour, brush on crackle medium (or a coat of PVA glue, a common substitute), and while it is still tacky, brush a top colour on in one direction. Cracks open as it dries, showing the base.

Homemade chalk-style paint

Ready-made chalk paint is often imported and costly. A widely shared home recipe mixes **plaster of Paris** with emulsion paint. Stir about **1 part plaster of Paris into 1 part cool water** until smooth with no lumps, then mix that paste into **3 parts emulsion paint**, all by volume. It gives a matt, slightly gritty finish that grips many surfaces and sands easily for distressing. Mix only what you will use in one session, because it thickens as it stands. Seal with clear wax or water-based varnish.

Plaster dust and sanding

Plaster of Paris and sanded paint make fine dust. Mix and sand outdoors or near an open window, wear a dust mask, and keep children away. Never pour leftover plaster mix down a sink: it hardens in pipes. Let it set in the container and dispose of it with solid waste.
Faux metal and gilding

A gold or bronze touch on a frame edge, a vase rim or carved details lifts a piece instantly. Use metallic acrylic paint applied with dry brushing, or **gilding**: brush a special size (adhesive), wait until it is tacky as the label directs, press on imitation gold leaf, then brush away the excess with a soft brush. Seal imitation leaf, because it can tarnish.
Always test on a sample

Keep a stack of scrap boards or cardboard. Before any client piece, test the colour pair and technique on a sample. Label the back with paints and steps used, and you build a finish library to show clients.

For small items, a 250 ml tin of emulsion goes a long way; you rarely need a full 4-litre bucket. Buy sample pots or share larger tins with other makers, and record how much each item used so your costing is accurate.

Stencils and printing blocks let you repeat a design many times with the same quality. That is what makes a matching set of cushions, napkins or wall borders possible, and what turns a hobby into production. This lesson covers making the tools from low-cost and upcycled materials, printing cleanly, and planning repeats with simple arithmetic.
A person creating a patterned artwork
A good stencil or block lets you repeat one design cleanly across a whole set.
Making a stencil
**Material**: clear acetate sheets, plastic folder covers or cleaned old X-ray film all work. They are thin, waterproof and can be washed and reused. Thick card works for a few prints only.
**Design**: draw a bold, simple shape. Fine lines and tiny gaps clog with paint.
**Bridges**: any closed shape (like the centre of an 'O' or a leaf) needs small strips, called bridges, that hold the inner piece in place. Make bridges at least 3 to 4 mm wide.
**Cutting**: tape the film over the drawing on a cutting board or thick cardboard and cut with a sharp craft knife, turning the board rather than your hand on curves.
Craft knife safety

Always cut away from your body and your other hand, use a metal ruler for straight lines, change blades when they drag, and close or cap the knife between cuts. Keep blades away from children and wrap used blades in tape before throwing them away.
Printing a clean stencil
Fix the stencil with masking tape or a light spray of repositionable adhesive so it cannot move.
Load a stencil brush or a piece of dense sponge with a small amount of paint.
**Off-load**: dab most of the paint onto paper towel until the brush is almost dry. Too much paint is the main cause of bleeding under the edges.
**Pounce**: dab straight up and down, building colour in two or three light layers rather than one heavy one.
Lift the stencil straight up, wipe its back, and move to the next position.
Block printing

Block printing uses a raised design that you ink and press down, like a stamp. You can carve **lino** or a **soft rubber carving block** with lino cutting tools, or make a quick block from craft foam glued onto a wooden off-cut. Remember that a block prints in **mirror image**: letters and asymmetrical shapes must be carved reversed. Roll ink or fabric paint thinly with a small roller (a brayer), press the block firmly, and lift straight up.

A pattern looks professional when it fits the item evenly, with no half-motif squeezed in at one edge. Measure the item, decide the motif size plus spacing, and divide. If it does not divide evenly, adjust the spacing, not the motif. Mark light pencil or chalk guide lines, or tape a strip of paper with marks along the edge as a registration guide.

Cement, air-dry clay and found objects let you make solid, sculptural décor: planters, candle holders, trinket dishes, wall pieces and framed assemblages. This module teaches correct mixes, moulds from waste containers, safe handling of cement, and how to compose objects into art.

Make two-part moulds from upcycled containers and release the cast cleanly

Cement planters, candle holders, bookends and coasters are popular modern décor, and the raw material is sold in every Nigerian building materials market. Strictly, cement mixed with only sand is **mortar**, and with sand plus gravel it is **concrete**; for small décor most makers use a sand and cement mix because fine sand gives smoother surfaces. Everyday speech calls all of it 'concrete', and so will this lesson.
A building brick
The same Portland cement used for building can be cast into small décor objects.
Cement can burn skin and eyes

Wet cement is strongly alkaline and can cause chemical burns and dermatitis; the dust irritates eyes, nose and lungs. Wear waterproof gloves (nitrile or rubber), safety goggles, a dust mask when pouring dry powder, and long sleeves. Mix outdoors or in a well-ventilated space. If wet cement gets on skin, wash it off promptly with plenty of clean water; if it gets in the eyes, rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical help. Never mix cement in food containers you will use again for food, and keep children and pets away.
Materials and moulds

**Cement**: ordinary Portland cement, sold in 50 kg bags. Buy a small quantity from a seller who splits bags if you only need a few kilograms, and keep it dry, because damp cement forms lumps and becomes useless.
**Sand**: fine, clean sharp sand, sieved through a kitchen sieve or mosquito net to remove stones and leaves.
**Moulds**: two containers, one inside the other, such as a large and small ice cream bucket, yoghurt cups, plastic bottles cut in half, or old food tins. Flexible plastic releases most easily.
**Release agent**: a thin coat of used cooking oil or petroleum jelly on every surface that touches the mix.
**Weights and spacers**: stones or sand to hold the inner mould down, and a cork or short pipe for a drainage hole.
The mix

A practical casting mix for small pieces is about **1 part cement to 2 parts fine sand by volume**. Some makers use 1 to 3 for a coarser, cheaper mix. Add water little by little and stir until it looks like **thick porridge**: it should hold a shape on the trowel but settle when you tap the container. Too wet and the piece is weak, cracks and shrinks; too dry and it will not fill the mould, leaving holes. Mix only what you can pour in about 20 to 30 minutes.

Casting step by step
Oil the inside of the outer mould and the outside of the inner mould.
For a planter, push an oiled cork or short pipe into the centre of the outer mould base to form a drainage hole.
Pour mix into the outer mould to about 2 cm deep for the base, then press the inner mould down onto it and centre it, leaving walls at least 1.5 to 2 cm thick.
Fill the gap between the moulds, tapping the sides firmly for a minute or two to release air bubbles.
Weigh the inner mould down with stones or sand so it cannot float up.
Cover with nylon and leave in shade for about 24 hours, then remove the moulds gently.
Worked example: four small planters
For example, Esther in Abuja wants to cast four planters, each with an outer mould of about 1 litre and an inner mould of about 0.5 litre.
Mix volume per planter = 1.0 - 0.5 = 0.5 litre of wall and base. Four planters need 4 x 0.5 = 2 litres.
Wet mix shrinks in volume compared to the dry ingredients, so she prepares about 2.5 litres of dry material.
At 1 cement : 2 sand, 2.5 litres is 3 parts, so 1 part is about 0.83 litre. She measures about 0.8 litre cement and 1.7 litres sand using a marked 1-litre cup.
She adds water a little at a time until it looks like thick porridge, records the water used, and pours all four in one session.
She demoulds after 24 hours and keeps the planters wrapped in damp cloth inside nylon for 7 days, wetting the cloth daily.
All four planters come out with smooth walls and drainage holes. Her written quantities let her repeat the batch exactly.
Curing and finishing

Cement hardens by a chemical reaction with water, not by drying. If a fresh piece dries out quickly in the sun or harmattan wind, it becomes weak and dusty. Keep it damp and covered for about a week. After that, sand rough edges with wet-and-dry paper, used wet to keep dust down. Fill small holes with a paste of cement and water. Paint with emulsion or acrylic, or leave the natural grey and seal with a clear masonry sealer if you want it water-resistant.
Before planting

New cement can make soil water very alkaline, which some plants dislike. Many makers soak finished planters in water for a few days, changing the water, before planting. Always include a drainage hole, or tell the buyer it is a cover pot for a plastic pot inside.

For candle holders, set a tealight or the empty cup it came in as the inner mould, so the hollow is the right size. Cement does not burn, but never leave lit candles unattended and tell buyers to place holders on a heat-proof surface away from curtains.

Dispose of leftover mix by letting it harden in a container and throwing it out as solid waste. Never rinse cement down drains or into gutters; it sets underwater and blocks them. Rinse tools in a bucket of water and let the sediment settle before pouring the clear water away.

Air-dry clay hardens at room temperature, so you need no kiln. It is ideal for trinket dishes, jewellery dishes, small vases for dried flowers, wall plaques, decorative beads and name tags. Because it is not fired, it stays sensitive to water: this one fact shapes how you finish it and what you tell buyers.

Making cold porcelain

Cold porcelain is a dough made from **cornstarch** (corn flour) and **white PVA glue**, with a little oil and an acid such as lemon juice or vinegar to help it keep. A commonly used recipe is **1 cup cornstarch, 1 cup PVA glue, 1 tablespoon vegetable or baby oil and 1 tablespoon lemon juice or white vinegar**. Mix everything in a non-stick pot, stir over low heat until it pulls away from the sides as one lump, then turn it out and knead with oiled hands as it cools. Wrap tightly in cling film and store in an airtight container.
Kitchen tools and heat

Use a pot and spoon kept only for crafts afterwards, because glue residue is not food-safe. The dough is hot when it comes off the heat: let it cool enough to handle, and keep children away from the stove. Wash hands after working with clay and glue.
Three ways to shape
**Pinch**: roll a ball, push your thumb into the centre and pinch the walls evenly while turning it. Good for small bowls and tealight cups (with a glass insert).
**Slab**: roll clay to an even thickness between two wooden strips about 5 mm thick. Cut shapes with a knife or a cutter, then press texture into them with lace, leaves or a stamp.
**Drape mould**: lay a slab over or inside an upturned saucer or bowl lined with cling film, trim the edge, and let it firm up before removing.

To join two pieces, **score** both surfaces with crosshatched scratches, brush on a little water (or for cold porcelain, a dab of PVA), press together and smooth the seam. Without scoring, joins often separate as the clay dries and shrinks.
Worked example: a set of six ring dishes
For example, Rahila in Makurdi makes ring dishes to sell as gifts in sets of three.
She rolls a slab 5 mm thick between two wooden strips and presses an old lace doily into it for texture.
She cuts six circles using a 10 cm diameter cup as a cutter.
She drapes each circle inside a cling-film-lined saucer so the edges curve up.
She dries them slowly, loosely covered with a cloth, turning them over after the first day so the bottoms dry too; total drying is about 3 days in her room.
She lightly sands edges, paints the rims with gold acrylic, and seals each dish with two coats of water-based varnish.
Six even dishes, packed as two sets of three. Her label says: decorative dish for rings and dry items, wipe with a dry cloth, not for food or water.
Drying without cracks
Keep thickness even: thick and thin parts dry at different speeds and crack where they meet.
Dry slowly out of direct sun and fan wind; harmattan air dries surfaces fast, so cover pieces loosely.
Turn flat pieces so both sides dry.
Small hairline cracks can be filled with a paste of the same clay and water (or PVA for cold porcelain), then sanded smooth once dry.
Expect some shrinkage, especially in cold porcelain; make pieces slightly bigger than the size you need.
Sealing and honest labelling

Seal every finished piece with acrylic varnish, water-based polyurethane or a clear sealer to protect it from humidity and handling. Even sealed, air-dry clay is **not waterproof** and is **not food-safe**. Vases for fresh flowers need a glass or plastic tube inside to hold water. Planters need a plastic pot inside. Say this on the label and in your product description, so a buyer is never disappointed.

Costing clay work is mostly about time, because the materials are cheap. Weigh or measure the clay used for one piece, note how long shaping, sanding and painting took, and remember that drying days tie up shelf space, not your hands. Making pieces in batches of six or more, all at the same stage on the same day, cuts the time per piece sharply compared with making one at a time.
Colour in the clay

Knead a little acrylic paint into cold porcelain before shaping to colour it all the way through. Wear gloves to keep your hands clean, and record how much paint you used per ball so colours match across a set.

Bottle caps, broken jewellery, keys, wood off-cuts, ankara scraps, old watch parts, shells and calabash pieces all become materials. Done well, it produces original wall art and mirror frames that no factory can copy. Done badly, it looks like glued rubbish. The difference is composition and craftsmanship.

Solvent-based contact adhesives are flammable and give off strong fumes: use them outdoors or with windows open, away from stoves and candles, and close the tin after use. Colour on cloth is at the heart of Nigerian décor, from kampala tie-dye to Yoruba adire. This module teaches fibre-reactive tie-dye, the three main adire resist methods, how to dye larger home textiles evenly by weight, and how to fix, wash and label dyed work so the colour lasts.

Tie-dye, often called **kampala** in Nigeria, works by **resist**: wherever fabric is tightly folded, tied or pressed, less dye reaches it, so it stays lighter. Many local dyers use vat dyes with caustic soda and sodium hydrosulphite. This lesson teaches a method that is easier to control at home and well documented by dye suppliers: **fibre-reactive dyes** fixed with **soda ash**, used cold on cotton.
A T-shirt
Cotton T-shirts and pillowcases are ideal first pieces for fibre-reactive tie-dye.
The right fabric and dye

Fibre-reactive dyes form a chemical bond with **plant fibres**: cotton, linen, rayon (viscose) and hemp. They do not dye polyester, and a polyester-cotton blend comes out pale. Old cotton bedsheets, T-shirts and plain shirting cloth bought by the yard are good, cheap materials. Wash new fabric first in hot water with detergent to remove factory finishes that block dye.
Four classic folds
**Spiral**: lay fabric flat, pinch the centre, twist into a flat round disc and tie with 3 or 4 rubber bands crossing in the middle like slices of a pie. Apply a different colour to each slice.
**Bullseye**: pinch the centre, pull up into a cone and tie bands at intervals down the cone. You get concentric rings.
**Stripes**: fold back and forth like a paper fan (accordion), then tie bands across. Fold straight for straight stripes or diagonally for diagonal stripes.
**Crumple (scrunch)**: scrunch the fabric randomly into a flat cake and tie it. Gives a marble-like texture, good for cushion covers.

Preparing solutions

**Soda ash soak**: soda ash (sodium carbonate) raises the pH so the dye can bond. Dye suppliers commonly recommend about 1 cup of soda ash per gallon (about 3.8 litres) of warm water. Dissolve, soak fabric for 15 to 20 minutes, then wring out until damp, not dripping.

**Dye solution**: wearing a dust mask and gloves, mix dye powder into a little warm water to a paste, then top up. A common squeeze-bottle strength is about 2 teaspoons of dye per cup of water for most colours, and more for black or very dark shades. Always check your supplier's chart.
**Apply**: squeeze dye onto the tied fabric section by section, pressing it into the folds. Turn it over and dye the back if you want full coverage.
**Batch**: wrap the wet piece in nylon so it stays damp and keep it somewhere warm for about 24 hours. In most of Nigeria room temperature is warm enough; in harmattan nights, keep it in a warm room.
Dust, alkali and utensils

Dye powders are fine and can irritate lungs and cause allergies, so wear a dust mask when measuring powder and mix where there is no breeze. Soda ash irritates skin and eyes: wear gloves and avoid splashes. Keep all dyeing cups, spoons and buckets for dyeing only, never for food, and store powders labelled, sealed and out of reach of children.

She washes the shirts in hot water with detergent and hangs them until just damp.
She dissolves 1 cup of soda ash in about 3.8 litres of warm water and soaks all six shirts for 20 minutes, then wrings them out.
She twists each shirt into a spiral and ties it into 6 sections with rubber bands.
She mixes two squeeze bottles, each about 2 teaspoons of dye in 1 cup of water, and alternates green and gold around the 6 sections.
She wraps each shirt in nylon and leaves them 24 hours, then rinses in cold water until the water runs nearly clear, removes the bands, and washes them together in hot water with a little detergent.
Six matching spiral shirts with clear green and gold sections. Very little colour runs in the final wash because she rinsed thoroughly first.
Rinsing out correctly

After batching, the fabric holds both bonded dye and loose dye that never bonded. If you open a wet piece and wash it in warm water straight away, loose dye can spread into white areas. Rinse first in **cold water**, with the ties still on, until the water runs fairly clear. Then remove ties and continue rinsing. Finally wash in **hot water** with detergent to remove the last loose dye, and dry in shade. You will learn a full colourfastness test in Lesson 4 of this module.

**Adire** is the indigo-dyed resist cloth of the Yoruba people of south-west Nigeria. The name is commonly explained as coming from **adi** (to tie) and **re** (to dye or soak). Abeokuta is often called the capital of adire making, with Ibadan and Osogbo also important centres. The craft grew in the early twentieth century when imported plain cotton shirting became widely available, declined later, and has been revived by artists and designers including Nike Davies-Okundaye.

Named eleko motifs include **Olokun**, linked with the goddess of the sea, **Ibadandun** ('Ibadan is sweet') and the **jubilee** pattern, among many others. When you use these motifs commercially, describe them correctly and credit the tradition. Better still, design your own motifs using the same methods, so your work is original.
Making each resist
**Oniko**: pinch a small point of cloth around a seed or pebble and wrap thread or raffia tightly around its base 6 to 10 times; knot it. Repeat in a grid or a scattered pattern.

**Alabere**: draw lines lightly in pencil, sew along them with strong thread in a running stitch about 5 mm long, leaving long tails. Pull every thread tight so the cloth gathers into firm pleats, and knot.

**Eleko**: cook a smooth, thick paste of cassava flour and water, cool it, and paint it onto stretched cloth with a brush or feather, or spread it through a stencil. Let it dry completely, usually a full day in sun or warm air.
Wet tied or stitched cloth in plain water before dyeing so the dye spreads evenly. For eleko, keep the cloth dry until it enters the dye.

How indigo works

Indigo does not dissolve in plain water. In a dye **vat** it is changed into a soluble, yellow-green form using an alkali and a reducing agent. Traditional dyers use fermented indigo leaves and ash lye; modern small dyers often use synthetic indigo with caustic soda and sodium hydrosulphite. When the cloth comes out of the vat it looks **yellow-green**, and within minutes in the air it turns **blue** as the dye oxidises. One dip gives pale blue; several dips, with airing between, give the deep blue that adire is known for.
Vat chemicals

Caustic soda is corrosive and causes severe burns; sodium hydrosulphite reacts with moisture and gives off irritating gas. If you use them, follow the supplier's instructions exactly, wear goggles, rubber gloves and long sleeves, work outdoors, add chemicals to water slowly (never water onto dry caustic soda), and store powders sealed and dry, away from children. A beginner can start with a ready-made indigo kit or work alongside an experienced dyer.
Worked example: an alabere and oniko table runner
For example, Yewande in Abeokuta makes a 35 x 150 cm cotton runner for a client's dining table.
She pre-washes the cotton and pencils 5 parallel lines along the length, 6 cm apart, leaving about 5.5 cm at each long edge: 4 gaps x 6 cm = 24 cm, and 35 - 24 = 11 cm, split into two 5.5 cm edges.
She stitches each line in running stitch and pulls the threads tight.
Between the lines she ties small oniko circles around seeds, every 10 cm along the runner.
She wets the cloth, dips it for about a minute, airs it until blue, and repeats for 4 dips in total.
She rinses, removes stitches and ties carefully with a seam ripper, then washes and irons it.
A runner with five fine white stitched lines and rows of small circles on deep blue, all from planned measurements.

Eleko paste softens in liquid, so dip eleko cloth briefly and let it dry or air between dips; long soaking lifts the paste and blurs the design. After the final dip and airing, soak the cloth in water and gently scrape or rub off the softened paste.

Modern décor uses adire beautifully as cushion covers, table runners, framed panels, lampshades and upholstery panels. A single strong motif panel framed on a wall, or a set of cushions in three different resist methods, makes a confident statement in a neutral room.

Dyeing home textiles is often an upcycling job: faded curtains, stained white tablecloths and dull cushion covers can all get a second life with a new colour. Larger items bring a new challenge, **even colour**. A blotchy curtain is hard to sell. Immersion dyeing, where the whole piece moves freely in a dye bath, gives the most even result, and accurate quantities by weight make results repeatable.
A bed with linen
Bed linen, curtains and cushions can be refreshed and upcycled with an even immersion dye.
Check what the fabric is

Read the label first. If there is none, cut a small snippet from a hidden seam and do a careful **burn test** outdoors, holding the snippet with tweezers over a non-flammable dish, away from anything that can catch fire. Cotton and linen burn with a smell like burning paper and leave soft grey ash. Polyester melts, shrinks away from the flame and leaves a hard bead. Fibre-reactive dye will only work well on the cotton-type result. Curtains with a rubbery blackout backing or a shiny coating are not good candidates.
Working by weight of fabric

Professional recipes are written as a **percentage of the dry fabric weight**, called depth of shade. Weigh the dry item on a kitchen or bathroom scale. Roughly, light shades use about 0.5 to 1% dye, medium shades about 2%, and dark shades 4% or more, but each dye and supplier differs, so use their chart and your dye diary. The **liquor ratio** is the weight of water to fabric. Allowing about 20 to 30 litres of water per kilogram of fabric (about 20:1 to 30:1) lets the piece move freely. Salt and soda ash are added per litre of water following the supplier's instructions.
Worked example: four cushion covers in a medium shade
For example, Nneka in Owerri upcycles four faded cotton cushion covers. Together they weigh 800 g dry. She wants a medium terracotta.
Dye: 2% of 800 g = 0.02 x 800 = 16 g of dye powder.
Water: at a 20:1 ratio, 800 g fabric needs 20 x 0.8 = 16 litres of water.
She checks her supplier's chart for salt and soda ash per litre and multiplies by 16 litres.
She dissolves the dye completely, adds it to the water with the salt, puts in the pre-wetted covers and stirs for the time on the chart before adding the dissolved soda ash.
She stirs often, every few minutes at first, for the full time on the chart, then rinses and washes as for tie-dye.
Four evenly dyed covers in one matching colour. Because she wrote down 2% and 20:1, she can repeat the shade for a fifth cover later.

Large pieces such as curtains
Weigh each curtain panel. If a panel is too big for your largest basin or drum, dye it alone and stir constantly rather than crowding it.
Remove hooks, rings and tape that could rust or resist dye; synthetic thread in seams may stay the old colour, which can look like a design detail.
Dye all panels for one window in one session from one batch of mixed dye, so they match.
Expect cotton to shrink slightly, especially if it has never been washed hot. Wash and measure first, and allow for it when making curtains to size.
Sun fades colour

Curtains take strong Nigerian sun every day, and many dyes fade in direct sunlight over time. Choose colours your supplier rates well for light fastness, suggest a lining to clients, and avoid promising that bright colours will never fade. Medium and darker shades usually show fading less than pale pastels.
Choosing colours for a room

Dyed textiles usually provide accent colour in a room. Pick one colour from a rug, painting or adire piece already in the room and repeat it in two or three textiles. Dye a small swatch first and look at it in the actual room in daylight and at night, because colours look different under warm LED bulbs. Keep the swatch pinned to your order sheet.
Big buckets, hot water

A bucket with 16 litres of water weighs about 16 kg. Fill it where you will use it, lift with bent knees or scoop water out first, and keep hot dye baths away from children. Dye outdoors or in a ventilated space, and wear gloves throughout.

Upcycled textiles sell better with a short note on the label: 'upcycled cotton, hand-dyed'. Be honest about any old stains that the dye covered but did not remove, since some may show faintly in certain light.

This lesson gives you simple home tests, the fixes for common problems, care labels buyers can follow, and responsible handling of leftover dye and chemicals.

Two simple tests

**Wash test**: put the dyed item, or a cut swatch, in a basin of warm water with a little detergent together with a small piece of white cotton. Leave 30 minutes, squeeze a few times, then compare the white cloth with an unused piece. Any staining means more washing out is needed.

**Rub test**: rub a dry white cotton cloth firmly back and forth on the dyed surface about 10 times, then repeat with a damp white cloth. Colour on the cloth means loose dye or unfixed surface colour.
Repeat the tests after any extra washing until the white cloth stays clean, or nearly so.

A batch only leaves your workshop after it passes both tests.
Worked example: a failed batch saved
For example, Aisha in Kano finishes 10 indigo-dyed napkins for a restaurant. In the rub test, the damp white cloth turns light blue.
She checks her notes: she aired each dip for only 2 minutes, and gave a short final rinse.
She soaks all 10 napkins in clean water for an hour, then washes them in hot water with detergent twice, rinsing well each time.
She dries them in shade and repeats both tests on two napkins.
The white cloth now shows only a very faint tint on the damp rub, so she writes 'wash separately for the first few washes' on the care card.
The batch is released with an honest care card instead of being rushed out, and her process notes now say to air each dip longer and wash twice.
Writing care labels

A good care label is short and specific. Include fibre content, dye method if useful (hand-dyed, indigo, tie-dye), washing temperature, and clear instructions. For most hand-dyed cotton décor, sensible instructions are: wash separately or with similar colours, use cool or warm water and mild detergent, do not use bleach, dry in shade, iron on the reverse. Use the internationally recognised textile care symbols if you know them well, but always add words too, because many buyers do not read the symbols.
Sample label: 100% cotton cushion cover, hand-dyed adire. Wash separately in cool water. No bleach. Dry in shade. Iron on reverse. Cushion insert not included.
Sew a small fabric label into seams, or attach a card tag with a ribbon for items like table runners.
Add your business name and WhatsApp number so satisfied buyers can reorder.
Responsible disposal

Used dye baths can contain alkali, salt and dye. Never pour them into streams, open gutters, near wells or boreholes, or onto vegetable gardens. Let solids settle, dilute with plenty of water and pour into a toilet or a sewer drain connected to a proper soak-away or sewer, away from water sources. Return unused chemicals to sealed, labelled containers. Follow any rules your state environmental agency sets for small workshops.

Keep a batch number on every order sheet and care card, for example 'IND-2026-07'. If a buyer ever reports a problem, you can look up exactly what you did, fix the process, and reassure the customer with facts, which builds trust.

Store finished stock folded in clean cotton bags or wrapped in plain paper, out of direct sun, and never in damp nylon, which can trap moisture and cause mildew spots during the rainy season. Keep different colours separated by paper until they are fully dry and tested, because damp deep blues and reds can mark lighter pieces they touch.
For decorative pieces that will rarely be washed, such as framed adire panels or wall hangings, say so on the label: 'spot clean only with a damp cloth' protects both the piece and you.

Upcycling means turning something old or discarded into something of **higher value**. Not every old item is worth the work. Strategic upcyclers choose pieces where a modest amount of effort and material creates a big jump in value, and pass on the rest. Used furniture markets, relocation sales, carpenters' off-cuts and items friends are throwing away are all good sources.

A solid old chair with a tired finish is a classic high-value upcycling project.

Prioritise high-value pieces; low-value, high-effort items rarely pay back the time.

Read the matrix as follows: the top row is high value added, the bottom row is low; the left column is low effort, the right column is high. A solid wood side table that only needs sanding and paint is a quick win. A sofa needing new foam and upholstery may be a big project worth planning. Turning jars into candle holders is a small extra to batch. A chipboard wardrobe with swollen, water-damaged panels is usually one to avoid.
Inspect before you buy
**Structure**: press down and rock the piece. Loose joints can be re-glued; cracked legs and swollen chipboard are hard to fix well.
**Pests**: look for small round holes, fine powder (frass) underneath, or mud tunnels that suggest termites. Do not bring infested furniture into a home or workshop.
**Material**: solid wood sands and repairs well. Chipboard and MDF swell if wet and cannot be sanded deeply. Laminate needs special primer.
**Old paint**: thick, layered old paint of unknown age may contain lead.
Lead in old paint

The World Health Organization warns that lead paint is a major source of lead exposure, especially harmful to children and pregnant women. Do not dry-sand, burn or heat-strip old paint of unknown age. Where you must remove it, wet-sand or use a chemical stripper outdoors following the label, wear a well-fitting dust mask and gloves, clean up with damp cloths rather than sweeping, and keep children and pregnant women away. If unsure, paint over a sound old finish after a light scuff instead of removing it.
The refinishing sequence
**Clean**: wash with warm water and detergent (or sugar soap) to remove grease and dirt; rinse and dry fully.
**Repair**: re-glue loose joints with wood glue and clamp or tie them overnight; fill holes and chips with wood filler.
**Sand**: start at 80 or 120 grit for rough areas, then 180 to 240 grit for a smooth finish, sanding with the grain.
**Prime**: use a primer that suits the surface, especially on bare wood, filler patches, laminate or metal.
**Paint**: two thin coats are better than one thick coat; follow the tin's recoat time.
**Seal**: protect tabletops and handles with clear varnish or polyurethane. Replace hardware such as knobs if needed.

Many talented makers lose money without noticing, because they price by guesswork or copy someone else. A sound price covers **everything** it cost you to make the piece, pays you for your time, and leaves a profit to grow the business. This lesson builds a price step by step, then covers where to sell and how to get paid safely.

The four parts of a price

Materials actually used
Materials form the base; labour, overheads and profit sit on top, and none can be skipped.
**Materials**: everything used in the piece, including small items such as glue, sandpaper, tags and packaging. Use what you actually used, from your records.
**Labour**: hours spent x an hourly rate you set for yourself. Decide a fair rate based on what you could earn elsewhere for skilled work.

**Overheads**: costs of running the business that are not in one piece: data, electricity or fuel, transport to market, tools that wear out. A simple method is to add a percentage, for example 10 to 15%, to materials plus labour, and check it against your real monthly overheads.
**Profit**: money for the business to grow, save and survive slow months.

For example, Halima from Module 1 prices her 45 cm diamond hanging. Prices are illustrative assumptions for this example only.
Materials: she assumes cord at 250 naira per metre and used about 44 m: 44 x 250 = 11,000. Dowel 1,500, hanging cord, tag and packaging 1,000. Materials = 13,500 naira.
Labour: about 3.1 hours x 2,000 naira per hour = 6,200 naira.
Profit at a 30% markup on cost: 0.30 x 21,670 = 6,501. Price = 21,670 + 6,501 = 28,171, which she rounds to 28,500 naira.
Her retail price is 28,500 naira. The profit of about 6,800 naira after rounding is about 24% of the price, so a 30% markup gives a margin of roughly a quarter.
Markup, margin and wholesale

**Markup** is profit as a percentage of cost. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of the selling price. They are not the same: a 30% markup is only about a 23% margin before rounding. Confusing them is a common way to underprice. If a shop or interior designer will resell your work, they need their own profit, so you offer a **wholesale price** below retail. A common convention is that the shop's retail price is around double the wholesale price, so your wholesale price must still cover your full cost plus some profit. If your full cost leaves no room for that, either make the piece faster, use materials more efficiently, or sell it only retail.

Never release goods on the strength of an SMS or a screenshot of a transfer: fake alerts are common. Confirm the money has actually arrived by checking your bank or wallet app. Be wary of 'overpayments' where the buyer asks you to refund the difference. Mix **textures**: smooth cement, soft macramé, glossy glaze, rough wood. Repeat one **colour** across the room in at least three places so it feels planned.

What you will learn

Macramé is making textiles by knotting cords. Every piece, from a key holder to a two-metre wall hanging, is a handful of knots repeated in patterns.
You will choose cord, master six knots, calculate cord, and finish pieces neatly enough to sell.
Choosing cord
Cord types and thickness
Single-strand cotton: fluffy fringes
3-ply cotton: hangings, wavy fringe
Braided cord: hangers that carry weight
Upcycled T-shirt yarn or ankara strips
4 to 5 mm suits most hangings and hangers
Single-strand cotton brushes into a soft, fluffy fringe, but frays as you work. 3-ply twisted cotton suits wall hangings and plant hangers. Tape its ends, or they unravel.
Braided cord is strong for hangers that carry weight. Upcycled T-shirt yarn or ankara strips make chunky baskets and mats, but the thickness varies.
3 mm cord suits coasters. 4 to 5 mm is the most common for hangings and hangers. Feel the cord first: cotton is soft and takes dye, nylon is slippery.
Six knots cover nearly everything
Lark's head: mounts cords on the dowel
Square knot: flat, over two filler cords
Half square knot: twists into a spiral
Double half hitch: raised lines
Overhand and gathering knots: ends, bundles
Even tension, not speed, makes work look professional.
The lark's head mounts each cord on the dowel or ring, folded in half, giving you two working strands.
The square knot uses four strands. The middle two are fillers that stay still. Tie one half, then the mirror half, and it lies flat.
Tie only the first half again and again, and it twists naturally into a spiral. That is the half square knot.
For a double half hitch, hold one cord tight as a guide, and wrap each working cord around it twice. A row makes a crisp line.
The overhand knot stops fringe ends. The gathering knot binds a bundle, at the top and bottom of plant hangers.
Hang your dowel at chest height and stand to work. Pull every knot with the same force.
Cord maths
Bisi cuts cord for a wall hanging
Finished length x 4: 60 x 4 = 240 cm
Folded, so x 2: 480 cm, or 4.8 m per cord
16 cords x 4.8 m = 76.8 m
Add about 10%: plan for 85 m, one batch

Running out of cord midway is the most common beginner frustration. For example, Bisi in Ibadan wants a hanging 60 cm long, with 16 cords. Each working strand needs about 4 times the finished length: 240 cm.
The lark's head folds each cord in half, so she cuts 480 cm, or 4.8 m, per cord. That is about 8 times the finished length.
16 cords times 4.8 m is 76.8 m.
She adds about 10% for mistakes, and plans for 85 m, all from one batch, so the colour matches. Dense knotting uses more. Keep notes, so your own rule improves.
Wall hangings
Plan three zones, then finish well
Header: holds the cords in order
Body: the pattern and focal point
Fringe: a V, a curve or a straight line
Count knots after every row
Photograph with measurements in the caption
Sketch the hanging first, in three zones. The header holds the cords in order. The body carries the pattern, such as diagonal hitch lines meeting in a diamond. The fringe gives shape.
A missed knot becomes obvious once the piece hangs, and is hard to undo. After each row, count the knots against your sketch, and look from two metres away.
Photograph it in daylight on a plain wall, and write the dowel width and total length in the caption. Buyers ask for size first.

Ceiling hook in a joist or beam
A card with maximum pot size
Never

Use a plastic hook

Never from a curtain rod or a plastic hook. And never over beds, baby cots or walkways, where someone could be hurt if it falls.

A plain tray, jar, stool or cushion can be transformed by its surface. Advanced decoupage has edges that disappear, no bubbles, and a surface smooth enough to wipe.

Prepare, apply, then bury the edge
Sand wood 120 then 180; light base coat
Use the thin printed layer of a napkin
Glue on the surface, smooth from centre
Thin coats, light wet sand after about four
Sand wood with 120, then 180 grit, and wipe off the dust. A white or light base coat makes prints show true colour.
Thin paper makes edges vanish. Peel the plain back layers off a printed napkin and keep only the top. Torn edges blend better than cut ones.
Brush a thin coat of medium, or PVA glue diluted about 3 parts glue to 1 part water, onto the surface, not the paper. Smooth from the centre outwards, through cling film, to push out air.
Then thin coats, each in a different direction. After about four, sand very gently with wet 400 grit paper, only flattening ridges, and keep coating.
Worked example
Funke's napkin serving tray
Sand, then two coats of white emulsion
Peel the napkin to the printed layer
Overlap torn edges by 1 cm
8 thin coats, wet-sand after coats 4 and 6
Label: decorative, wipe clean only
For example, Funke in Abeokuta upcycles an old wooden tray. She sands it, paints two coats of white emulsion, and peels two leaf napkins down to the printed layer.
She glues one half at a time, smoothing through cling film, and overlaps the torn edges by 1 cm.
She builds 8 thin coats of water-based varnish over two days, wet-sanding after coats 4 and 6. No napkin edges show. She labels it decorative, for dry items and wiping only.
Faux finishes
Five paint effects to master
Dry brushing: highlights raised parts
Colour wash: 1 part paint to 3 or 4 water
Sponging: a stone look
Distressing: sand edges to show dark base
Crackle: top coat over tacky medium
Every faux finish layers a base colour and a contrasting top colour. For dry brushing, wipe almost all paint off the brush, then sweep lightly. Paint catches only the raised parts.
A colour wash thins paint with water so the wood grain shows. Sponging dabs a second colour, rotating the sponge to avoid a repeating mark.
Distressing sands the edges and corners to reveal a dark base. For crackle, brush the top colour over crackle medium, or PVA glue, while it is still tacky. Never mix water-based and oil-based paint.
Grace mixes chalk-style paint
Recipe: 1 plaster, 1 water, 3 emulsion
Plans 800 ml: 800 / 5 = 160 ml per part
160 ml plaster + 160 ml water, smooth
Mix into 480 ml emulsion; stir between coats
Ready-made chalk paint is costly. A home recipe uses 1 part plaster of Paris, 1 part cool water, and 3 parts emulsion paint, by volume.
For example, Grace in Jos needs about 750 ml for two stools. To be safe she plans for 800 ml. That is 5 parts, so 160 ml per part.
She stirs 160 ml of plaster into 160 ml of water until smooth, then mixes it into 480 ml of emulsion. It thickens, so she stirs before coat 2.
Safety
Three safety rules for surfaces
Decoupage is not food-safe and softens if soaked. Never sell decoupage plates, bowls or cups for eating.
Mix and sand outdoors or by an open window, wear a dust mask, keep children away. Never pour plaster down a sink.
Cut away from your body and other hand, use a metal ruler, cap the knife, wrap used blades in tape.
PVA glue and most varnishes are not tested as safe for food. Decorate only the back of clear glass plates or the outside of jars, and label items: wipe clean, do not soak, decorative use.
Plaster and sanded paint make fine dust. Work outdoors or by an open window, wear a dust mask, and keep children away. Never pour leftover plaster down a sink.
When cutting stencils, always cut away from your body and your other hand.
Repeat patterns
Chioma's four cushion covers
45 cm cover, 1 cm border: 43 cm to print
5 motifs of 7 cm = 35 cm
8 cm left for 4 gaps: 2 cm each
Wash and iron first; chalk the grid
Dry 24 hours, then heat-set with an iron
Off-load the brush. Too much paint makes it bleed.

A pattern looks professional when it fits evenly, with no half-motif squeezed in at one edge. For example, Chioma in Enugu prints cushion covers 45 cm square. With a 1 cm border on each side, she has 43 cm to print.
Her block is 7 cm. Five motifs take 35 cm, leaving 8 cm for 4 gaps: 2 cm each. If it does not divide evenly, adjust the gaps, not the motif.
She washes and irons the covers first, marks a chalk grid, and after 24 hours drying, heat-sets them as the paint label directs.

Remember
Thin paper, torn edges, many thin coats
Base plus contrasting top colour
Chalk paint: 1 plaster, 1 water, 3 emulsion
Adjust gaps so repeats fit

Cement, air-dry clay and found objects let you make solid décor: planters, candle holders, trinket dishes and framed wall pieces.

Safety first
Waterproof gloves, safety goggles, a dust mask for dry powder, long sleeves. Mix outdoors.
Wash skin promptly with clean water. Eyes: rinse at least 15 minutes and seek medical help.
Never rinse cement down drains. Let leftovers harden and throw out as solid waste.
Wet cement is strongly alkaline. It can burn skin, and the dust irritates eyes and lungs. Wear waterproof gloves, goggles, a dust mask for dry powder, and long sleeves. Keep children and pets away.
If wet cement gets on skin, wash it off promptly with plenty of clean water. If it gets in the eyes, rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes, and seek medical help.
Never rinse cement down drains. It sets underwater and blocks them. And never mix it in food containers you will use for food again.

Oil both moulds; cork for drainage
Base about 2 cm; walls 1.5 to 2 cm thick
Tap out bubbles; weigh the inner mould
Demould after about 24 hours

Use two nesting containers, like ice cream buckets. Oil every surface that touches the mix, and push an oiled cork into the base for a drainage hole.
Pour a base about 2 cm deep, press in the inner mould, and keep walls at least 1.5 to 2 cm thick.
Tap the sides for a minute or two to release air, weigh the inner mould down with stones, cover, and demould gently after about 24 hours.

Cold porcelain
Cornstarch, PVA, oil, lemon
Smooth and fine
Cheap, sold locally

Colour on cloth is at the heart of Nigerian décor, from kampala tie-dye to Yoruba adire. Both work by resist: where fabric is tightly tied, less dye reaches it.
You will learn tie-dye, the three adire methods, even dyeing of larger textiles, and how to test and label your work.
Tie-dye
Ifeoma's six spiral T-shirts
Pre-wash 100% cotton in hot water

Twist a spiral, tie into 6 sections

Wrap in nylon; batch 24 hours warm

Fibre-reactive dyes bond with cotton, linen and rayon, but not polyester. For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha dyes six white 100% cotton T-shirts. She washes them first, to remove factory finishes.
She dissolves 1 cup of soda ash in about 3.8 litres of warm water and soaks the shirts for 20 minutes. Soda ash lets the dye bond.
She twists each shirt into a spiral, ties 6 sections, and squeezes on green and gold dye, each about 2 teaspoons per cup of water.
She wraps each shirt in nylon and leaves it warm for 24 hours. The soak and the wait make the colour permanent.
Then she rinses in cold water, ties still on, until the water runs nearly clear. Only then does she untie and wash hot, so loose dye cannot spread into the white areas.

Gives white circles and rings
Alabere: stitches pulled tight

Dip briefly; paste softens
Adire is Yoruba indigo resist cloth, rooted in Abeokuta, Ibadan and Osogbo. Oniko ties seeds or pebbles into the cloth. Alabere sews lines of running stitch, then pulls them tight.

Indigo colours in the air, not in the bath. For example, Yewande in Abeokuta wets her stitched runner and dips it for about a minute. It comes out yellow-green.
Within minutes in the air it turns blue. She repeats for 4 dips in total. One dip gives pale blue, and several give adire's deep blue.

Vat chemicals are dangerous. Caustic soda causes severe burns. Wear goggles, rubber gloves and long sleeves, work outdoors, and add chemicals to water slowly. A beginner can start with a ready-made kit, or work alongside an experienced dyer.
Even dyeing
Nneka dyes four cushion covers
Check it is cotton, not polyester
Weigh dry: 800 g
Water 20:1: 16 litres
Pre-wet, dissolve fully, stir often
A blotchy curtain is hard to sell. First check the fibre. In a careful burn test outdoors, cotton smells like burning paper and polyester melts into a hard bead.
Then work by weight. For example, Nneka in Owerri has four cushion covers weighing 800 g dry. For a medium shade she uses 2%, which is 16 g of dye.
At a 20 to 1 ratio, she needs 16 litres of water, so the covers can move freely. She pre-wets them, dissolves the dye fully, and stirs often. Dye all matching items in one batch.
Safety
Dust, heavy buckets and disposal
Dust mask when measuring powder, gloves for soda ash. Utensils for dyeing only, never food.
16 litres weighs about 16 kg. Fill it where you use it, lift with bent knees, keep hot baths from children.
Never into streams, gutters, near wells or boreholes, or onto vegetable gardens.

Dye powders can irritate lungs and cause allergies, so wear a dust mask when measuring. Soda ash irritates skin and eyes, so wear gloves. Keep every dyeing cup and bucket for dyeing only, never for food.
A bucket with 16 litres of water weighs about 16 kg. Fill it where you will use it, and lift with bent knees.
Never pour used dye baths into streams, open gutters, near wells or boreholes, or onto vegetable gardens.
Before you sell
Aisha saves a failed batch
Wash test: 30 minutes with white cotton
Rub test: dry, then damp, about 10 times
Pass: care label and batch number
Test every batch. Wash a swatch for 30 minutes with a small piece of white cotton. Then rub a dry, then a damp, white cloth on the surface about 10 times. Colour on the white cloth means loose dye.
For example, Aisha in Kano dyes 10 indigo napkins, and the damp cloth turns light blue. She soaks them, washes them hot twice, and tests again.
Now there is only a faint tint. She writes wash separately for the first few washes on the care card, instead of rushing the batch out.
Key points
Remember
Fibre-reactive dye: cotton, not polyester
Soda ash plus 24 warm hours fix colour
Rinse cold before untying
Work by dry weight: dye % and 20:1 water
Wash and rub test before every sale

To remember. Use cotton-type fabric. Soda ash and 24 warm hours fix the colour. Rinse cold before untying. Work by dry weight for even colour. And test every batch, then write a care label in words, not only symbols.

Upcycling means turning something old into something of higher value. But not every old item is worth the work. You will learn to choose wisely, and refinish safely.
Then you will price handmade décor so every sale makes a profit, get paid safely, and offer styling services that show off your own pieces.
Choosing projects
A solid wood side table that only needs sanding and paint: modest effort, big value added.
Rock it. Look for small holes, fine powder or mud tunnels that suggest termites.
A chipboard wardrobe with swollen, water-damaged panels rarely pays back the time.
Strategic upcyclers choose pieces where a modest effort creates a big jump in value. A solid wood side table that only needs sanding and paint is a quick win.
Before you buy, rock the piece. Loose joints can be re-glued, but cracked legs are hard to fix. Look for small holes, fine powder or mud tunnels. Never bring termites home.
Solid wood sands and repairs well. Chipboard swells when wet, so a water-damaged chipboard wardrobe is usually one to avoid.
Safety
Never dry-sand, burn or heat-strip it
Wet-sand or use stripper outdoors
Dust mask and gloves
Clean with damp cloths, not a broom
Keep children and pregnant women away from old paint work.
Thick, layered old paint of unknown age may contain lead. The World Health Organization warns that lead is especially harmful to children and pregnant women. Never dry-sand, burn or heat-strip it.

If you must remove it, wet-sand or use a chemical stripper outdoors, wear a well-fitting dust mask and gloves, and clean up with damp cloths. If unsure, paint over a sound old finish after a light scuff.
Keep children and pregnant women away. And for paints and varnishes, work outdoors or with windows open, away from flames.
Refinishing
Patience's bedside cabinet
Clean, then repair joints and holes
Sand 80 or 120, then 180 to 240 grit
Prime, two thin coats, then seal
Time: 7 hours. Before and after photos.
For example, Patience in Lagos buys a solid wood bedside cabinet for 8,000 naira. She washes off the grease, re-glues loose joints, and fills chips with wood filler.
She sands with the grain, from coarse to fine.
Then she primes, paints two thin coats rather than one thick one, and seals the top with varnish. She lines the drawer with leftover adire, a detail buyers notice.
Her materials come to 11,500 naira, so her full spend is 19,500 naira, plus 7 hours of work. And she photographs it before and after, from the same spot, in the same light.
Pricing
Halima prices her diamond hanging
For example, Halima prices her 45 cm macramé hanging from Module 1.
Labour: about 3.1 hours
Overheads: 10%
Profit: 30% markup on cost
She rounds to 28,500. Prices are illustrative.
Many talented makers lose money because they price by guesswork. A sound price has four parts. For example, Halima prices her diamond wall hanging.
Materials actually used: about 44 m of cord, the dowel, tag and packaging. That is 13,500 naira.
Labour: about 3.1 hours at 2,000 naira an hour, 6,200 naira.
Overheads, like data, transport and tools, at 10%: 1,970 naira. Her full cost is 21,670 naira.
A 30% markup adds 6,501 naira, and she rounds the price to 28,500 naira.
Markup is profit on cost. Margin is profit on price. Her profit is only about 24% of the price. Confusing the two is a common way to underprice.
Getting paid safely
Selling and delivery
Do
Confirm money in your own app
Use payment links or POS records
Take about half as deposit
Pack tightly; photograph the box
Never
Trust an SMS or screenshot alone
Refund an overpayment
Buy materials before a deposit
Cut price below your full cost

Confirm the money has actually arrived in your bank or wallet app. Payment links and POS payments give you a record. For custom work, take a deposit, often half, before you buy materials. Wrap fragile pieces and fill every gap in the box.
Never release goods because of an SMS or a screenshot. Fake alerts are common. Be wary of buyers who overpay and ask for a refund. And never cut your price below your full cost.
Styling
Vignettes and a styling package
Odd numbers, often three
High, medium and low heights
Mix textures; repeat one colour
Zainab: products, labour, transport
50% deposit; written photo permission

A vignette is a small styled group on a shelf or side table. Group objects in odd numbers, vary the heights, mix textures like smooth cement and soft macramé, and repeat one colour in at least three places.
For example, Zainab in Abuja styles a short-let flat with her own pieces. Products, styling time and transport come to 152,500 naira. She offers 150,000 if she can use the photos in her portfolio.
She takes a 75,000 naira deposit to start. She gets written permission for photos, and leaves out house numbers and family photos to protect the client's privacy.
Key points
Remember
High value, modest effort projects
Never dry-sand old paint
Materials + labour + overheads + profit
Confirm payment in your app
Style in odd numbers and varied heights

To remember. Choose projects with high value and modest effort. Never dry-sand old paint. Build every price from materials, labour, overheads and profit. Confirm payment in your own app. And show your pieces styled in real rooms.
